sources.title: Human History Map, imported civilization index
sources.note: Primary project data checked locally for the exact taiwan record, its approximate 1492-1530 display lifetime, and the separate taiwanese-tribes, dutch-formosa, taiwan-1878 and taiwan-1945 records. These are imported atlas identities, not proof of historical statehood or exact event dates.

sources.title: Human History Map, world-1492 historical border snapshot
sources.note: Primary project TopoJSON decoded locally. The taiwan feature covers 1492-1500 as one 138-vertex polygon with a simplified main-island outline. Point tests and bounds are preserved in identity.json; Penghu, Green Island, Orchid Island and Kinmen fall outside.

sources.title: Human History Map, world-1500 historical border snapshot
sources.note: Primary project TopoJSON decoded locally. The 1500-1530 feature has only 29 vertices and unexpectedly excludes tested coastal points including Tamsui, Keelung, Hualien, Taitung and Hengchun while retaining inland and western points. This is treated as a geometry artifact, not a historical contraction.

sources.title: Human History Map, separate modern Taiwan card
sources.note: Primary project card checked locally to prevent conflation. The modern taiwan-1945 record begins in 1945 and covers separate twentieth- and twenty-first-century political, social and economic history.

sources.title: Paul Jen-kuei Li, Elizabeth Zeitoun and Rik De Busser, Taiwan and the Formosan Languages
sources.note: 2024 Brill handbook chapter hosted by Academia Sinica, checked for Taiwan before the seventeenth century, the absence of one central authority, community diversity, trade and intermarriage, the Austronesian language family, early documentation, and the reconstructed Proto-Austronesian form *zalan, road. Modern classifications are not projected backward as exact 1500 ethnic borders.

sources.title: Technological Innovation and Social Unchange: Iron in Later Prehistoric Taiwan
sources.note: Open Journal of World Prehistory synthesis checked for late prehistoric ironworking, long-distance exchange, Chinese ceramics from the late first millennium, household-scale production, Heping Dao postholes and metallurgical remains, political variation and the limits of equating new technology with centralized hierarchy.

sources.title: Leigh K. Jenco, Chen Di’s Record of Formosa (1603) and an Alternative Chinese Imaginary of Otherness
sources.note: Historical Journal article checked for the date, setting and interpretive limits of Chen Di’s short 1603 eyewitness text, including diverse communities, marriage and work observations, deer hunting, burial, the absence of writing among his hosts and the title Dongfan ji. Chen was a visiting Ming literatus, not a neutral voice or a witness to every island community.

sources.title: National Museum of Taiwan Literature, Chen Di writes Dongfan ji
sources.note: Official literature knowledge-base entry checked for the January 1603 anti-pirate expedition, Chen Di’s limited visit, the approximately 1,500-character Dongfan ji, its southwestern geographic scope and its descriptions of villages, farming, clothing, food, gatherings, marriage and work. The museum stresses that much may have come from interviews rather than direct observation.

sources.title: National Museum of Prehistory, Taiwan Prehistory Hall
sources.note: National museum exhibition guide checked for at least 30,000 years of human history, repeated migration and regional adaptation, early farming and pottery, later iron technology, and exchange that brought bronze, glass and agate. Broad exhibition periods are used as background, not as exact biographies of people in 1500.

sources.title: Shihsanhang Museum of Archaeology, 2018 Annual Report: permanent exhibition
sources.note: Official museum annual report checked for its permanent exhibition’s northern Taiwan evidence: iron smelting, stone and bone tools, patterned pottery, beads, bronze, glass, gold and silver exchange goods, and animal remains including deer, boar, fish, birds and shellfish. One site cannot represent the whole island.

sources.title: Shihsanhang Museum of Archaeology, Anthropomorphic Jar
sources.note: Official artifact catalog checked for the red-brown jar’s face, dotted and circular decoration, approximate 1,800-500-year age range, burial context and status as the only human-faced jar found in Taiwan. Its possible religious significance remains an interpretation.

sources.title: National Museum of Prehistory, Archaeological Sites of the Tainan Science Park
sources.note: Museum research article checked for the long southwestern cultural sequence and Niaosong evidence including differently sized settlements, rice and Job’s tears, iron tools and a distinctive burial practice; later Siraya layers contain more iron, traded stoneware and porcelain, worked antler and glass ornaments.

sources.title: Encountering the Wider World before the Transition to History: Chinese Ceramics in Proto-historic Taiwan
sources.note: Academic archaeology chapter checked for Chinese ceramics and exchange from the tenth through sixteenth centuries, older Austronesian exchange routes and the caution that major maritime routes could pass Taiwan while contacts remained selective and uneven.

sources.title: Pietrusewsky and Tsang, A Preliminary Assessment of Health and Disease in Human Skeletal Remains from Shi San Hang
sources.note: Peer-reviewed Anthropological Science article checked for its deliberately small sample of 23 well-preserved adult skeletons from the broadly dated Shihsanhang site, low observed rates of cavities and abscesses, enamel and orbital stress markers, rare trauma, and the authors’ preliminary-health conclusion. The sample does not establish island-wide medicine or mortality.

sources.title: Bureau of Cultural Heritage, Beinan Archaeological Site and Dulan Mountain
sources.note: Official heritage dossier checked for eastern Taiwan’s much earlier Beinan settlement, houses, storage rooms and drainage ditches, plus the later Iron Age transition. It is used only to demonstrate what archaeology can sometimes recover and why those earlier drains cannot be called 1500-era toilets.

sources.title: Tonio Andrade, How Taiwan Became Chinese, Chapter 1: Taiwan on the Eve of Colonization
sources.note: Open Columbia University Press chapter checked for early seventeenth-century observations of deer hunting, dried meat, deerhide uses, clothing and trade, and the wider Chinese-Japanese maritime setting. Its quoted European and Chinese observers used period prejudices; their local reports are not treated as island-wide ethnography for 1492.

sources.title: National Museum of Taiwan History, Transcending 1624: Taiwan and the World
sources.note: National museum exhibition text checked for growing mid-sixteenth-century maritime connections, the Dutch arrival in 1624, the Spanish arrival in 1626, colonial competition, cultural exchange and the need to tell contact history from Taiwan-centered as well as outside perspectives.

proposedOverrides.name: Taiwan
proposedOverrides.summary: Taiwan around 1492-1530: diverse communities, village politics, ironworking, trade, family life, language, health clues, and mysterious toilets.

batchIdentityNotes: Exact target: taiwan, indexed approximately 1492-1530. It is distinct from taiwanese-tribes, dutch-formosa, taiwan-1878 and the already researched modern taiwan-1945 record.

Decoded world-1492 and world-1500 features are inconsistent simplified main-island polygons. Named point tests, bounds and vertex counts are recorded in identity.json; the geometry is not interpreted as a historical state boundary.

The narrative centers the atlas interval and clearly marks archaeology, the near-period 1603 outsider account, later comparison evidence and atlas gaps. No local Indigenous writing, school, medicine or toilet practice is invented where evidence is absent.
